content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Cereal, Multigrain, Ready-to-Eat is a nutritious blend of whole grains (oats, rice, wheat, corn) fortified with vitamins, specially formulated for children from 6 months old. The cereal has a soft texture, dissolves easily in milk or water, and requires no cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend contains several grain types, providing a broader range of nutrients.
The product meets strict quality standards and complies with infant‑food regulations in the EU and the US.
No artificial colors, flavors, or preservatives are added.
Each serving is enriched with iron, zinc, and B‑vitamins essential for growth and development.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and features a convenient dispenser.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The multigrain mix supplies steady energy needed for an active toddler.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Iron supports hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia in young children.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B6 aid normal nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Promote the development of strong bones and teeth during early growth.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Supports healthy digestion and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Children with known allergies to wheat, oats, or corn should be evaluated by a pediatrician before introducing the product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: While no added sugar is present, some versions may contain small amounts of natural sugars.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 6 months
items.content: Younger infants may have an immature digestive system, so introduction is recommended after six months.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one serving (about 30 g) with 120 ml of warm breast milk, formula, or water. Stir thoroughly until smooth. Serve immediately while warm.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal tightly and use within 4 weeks. Discard if any off‑odor, mold, or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Natto is a traditional Japanese fermented soybean product made by inoculating soybeans with the bacterium Bacillus subtilis var. natto. It has a sticky texture, strong aroma, and a mildly nutty flavor. Natto is commonly served over rice, used in salads, sushi, and as a supplement to various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Natto is one of the oldest fermented foods in Japan, with a history spanning over a thousand years.
The bacterium Bacillus subtilis produces the enzyme nattokinase, which is known to help thin the blood.
In Japan, natto is traditionally eaten for breakfast, often with soy sauce, mustard, and chopped green onions.
There are several regional varieties of natto that differ in taste, texture, and bean preparation methods.
Natto is exceptionally rich in vitamin K2 (menaquinone), a nutrient rarely found in other foods.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K2
items.content: Vitamin K2 plays a key role in regulating calcium deposition in bones and blood vessels, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of probiotics
items.content: Bacillus subtilis promotes a healthy gut microbiome and may improve digestion.

items.title: Contains complete protein
items.content: Natto provides plant‑based protein with all essential amino acids, beneficial for vegetarians.

items.title: High in enzymes
items.content: Enzymes such as nattokinase may help maintain healthy blood flow and reduce clot risk.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Soy isoflavones have antioxidant properties and may support hormonal balance.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should avoid natto as it can trigger reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared natto products often contain soy sauce, increasing the salt level.

items.title: Possible foodborne issues
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of unwanted bacteria and spoilage.

items.title: Effect on blood clotting
items.content: Because of nattokinase, individuals on anticoagulant medication should consume natto with caution.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Natto is typically served over hot rice, drizzled with soy sauce, mixed with mustard and finely chopped green onions. It can also be added to salads, rolls, omelets, or blended into smoothies as a nutritional boost.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store natto in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Cherry pie is a baked dessert consisting of a flaky crust filled with fresh or canned cherries sweetened with sugar and flavored with vanilla or cinnamon. The crust is usually crisp, while the filling is juicy and slightly tart.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cherry pie is considered a classic American dessert, especially popular during the summer season.
Traditional recipes often feature a double crust – bottom and top, sometimes with a lattice design.
Cherries are rich in antioxidants, particularly anthocyanins, which give them their bright red color.
In the United States, cherry pie is frequently served with a scoop of vanilla ice cream – "à la mode".
The dish likely originated in Europe in the 19th century when cherries became widely available.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cherries contain anthocyanins that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Cherries provide vitamin C, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in cherries promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many desserts, cherry pie can be made with modest amounts of butter.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional pies contain a lot of sugar, which can be an issue for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The crust usually contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tart cherries may irritate the stomach of individuals with high acidity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pie is fairly calorie‑dense due to crust and sugar; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cherry pie warm, often with a scoop of vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, or a light dusting of powdered sugar. Cut into portions and keep refrigerated for up to 3 days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the pie in an airtight container in the refrigerator. It can also be frozen for up to 2 months; reheat in the oven at 180 °C before serving to restore a crisp crust.

rice-brown-with-gravy-fat-added.title: Brown Rice with Gravy and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained by removing only the outer husk. When cooked with gravy and added fat, it gains a rich flavor and higher energy density.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ layers, making it more nutritious than white rice.
It provides more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as magnesium and phosphorus.
Cooking with gravy and fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins like vitamin E.
In several cultures, brown rice with sauce is a traditional festive dish.
Its antioxidant content is higher than that of most refined grains.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium contributes to normal muscle and nerve function and participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress and may reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Heart‑friendly when balanced
items.content: The healthy fats in the gravy can improve lipid profiles when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in rice deliver a steady release of energy, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat and gravy increase the dish’s calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared gravies can be high in salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Additive sensitivity
items.content: Some sauces contain flavor enhancers or preservatives that can trigger sensitivities.

items.title: Gluten risk
items.content: If the gravy is thickened with wheat flour, the dish may not be suitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice hot as a side dish with meat, poultry, or vegetables. Pair it with tomato, mushroom, or creamy gravies, and add a drizzle of olive oil or butter for extra richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with gravy should be cooled quickly and stored in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Sunflower seeds are the edible seeds of the sunflower plant (Helianthus annuus). They have a mild nutty flavor, a crunchy texture, and are typically sold without added salt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower is one of the most widely cultivated crops worldwide, and its seeds are a major source of vegetable oil.
The seeds are rich in vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant.
Seeds can be used both as food and in cosmetics (oil for skin and hair).
There are several seed varieties: large ones for snacking and smaller ones for oil production.
Sunflowers attract bees and other pollinators, supporting biodiversity.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E protects cells from oxidative stress and supports skin health.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat is polyunsaturated, including omega‑6 fatty acids important for heart health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Protein supports muscle maintenance, while fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium contributes to immune function and protects against free radicals.

items.title: Seed allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sunflower seeds.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Seeds are calorie-dense, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking can lower its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sunflower seeds can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, oatmeal, baked goods, or used to make homemade oil. Eating them unsalted helps control sodium intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
